content:
Something wasn't clear to me while reading the manual at 7.6.3.7. Theory and Construction. Does a termination proof consist of showing the motive can be satisfied by a term that is an application of Wellfounded.fix? I.e., is a termination proof a proof that the function can be rewritten in the form, e.g.,

noncomputable def div (n k : Nat) : Nat :=
  (inferInstance : WellFoundedRelation Nat).wf.fix
    (fun n r =>
      if h : k = 0 then 0
      else if h : k > n then 0
      else 1 + (r (n - k) <| by
        show (n - k) < n
        omega))
    n

as in the manual? I wasn't able to make sense of how this example related to what's happening when a function that needs to be proven to be terminating doesn't take this form. Is it elaborated to this for the kernel?

I am still interested in this! The manual doesn't seem to be very clear on this; is the point of the wellfounded recursion API ultimately to elaborate functions into WellFounded.fix terms, this being the final representation of a recursive function in the kernel?

Yeah elaborating wellfounded recursion essentially means bringing it into this form, or more precisely,

  • preprocessing (e.g. turning if ... into if h : ...) to get more assumption to use for termination
  • packing arguments into a tuple (if there are multiple varying arguments)
  • packing arguments into a sum type (if there are multiple mutual functions)
  • find out a working termination measure (if none is provided)
  • constructing the measure on this new type
  • rewriting all recursive occurrences to an application of the "inductive hypothesis" given in WellFounded.fix
  • collecting all goals that arise from proofs that it's decreasing
  • run the user-provided tactic (or the default one)
  • declare all the functions in the mutual block as wrappers around the sum-tuple-packed version (which is usually called functionName._unary or functionName._mutual)
I see, thanks a lot for the answer, that makes a lot of sense!
